title: Leaders Who Discount Long-Term Rewards and Risks
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article applies the behavioral economics concept of temporal discounting, the tendency to overvalue immediate rewards and undervalue delayed ones, to leadership and goal-setting. When leaders chase quick wins at the expense of longer-range objectives, teams learn that only near-term priorities actually matter, creating a misalignment that undermines long-term success. The piece also notes that discounting distorts risk perception, causing leaders to underweight dangers that are still a long way off. Its recommended countermeasures include talking frequently about long-term aspirations and deliberately committing resources to initiatives like talent development that won't pay off immediately.
points: Temporal discounting is the tendency to value immediate rewards far more than larger, delayed ones
The bias affects risk perception too, causing people to underweight dangers that are still far off
Leaders who chase short-term wins teach teams that only near-term priorities really count
Countermeasures include talking about long-term goals often and investing resources in things like talent development ahead of need
quotes: Temporal discounting is the process by which a person values immediate rewards more highly than rewards that are delayed or given in the future, even when those rewards are larger or more beneficial.
This tendency explains why people sometimes make impulsive decisions, choosing short-term gratification over long-term gain.
Leaders who succumb to the effects of discounting prioritize short-term outcomes while often sacrificing future objectives and gains.
They also commit resources to longer-term initiatives, such as talent development, innovation, and process improvement, to offset any attempt at discounting.
Temporal discounting is yet another enemy of great leadership and decision-making.
